senses.gloss:
āsanamūrti
(‘image in the seated posture’)
------------------------------------------
The Hindu temple is an ancient institution. The images that are installed inside the shrines or inscribed on the walls and the pillars should be prepared strictly according to the rules of ‘mūrtiśilpaśāstra’ or इचोनोग्रफ्य्. Such mūrtis or images of gods and goddesses are generally divided into three kinds depending upon their posture: the स्थानक or standing, the आसन or sitting and the śayana or lying down.
The āsanamūrtis again can be of various types depending on the particular आसन or posture adopted. At least twenty āsanas are mentioned in the iconographical works. To name a few: ālīḍha, कूर्म, ध्यान, पद्म, paryaṅka, योग, bhadra, vīra and स्वस्तिक.

Āṣāḍha
------------------------------------------
The fourth month of the Hindu lunar चलेन्दर् is called आषाढ (June-July) when the full-मोओन् is said to be near the constellation Āṣāḍhā. The एकादशी (11th day) of the bright fortnight of this month is christened ‘śayanī’ since it was believed that Lord विष्णु went to bed on this day, to wake up again on the एकादशी of kārttika bright fortnight, called ‘prabo-dhinī or bodhinī.’ The legend of विष्णु’s going to bed for four months might be symbolic of the disappearance of the sun (who is also विष्णु) behind the clouds during the rainy season.
The deity सुब्रह्मण्य (also known as षण्मुख and स्कन्द) is associated with this month. The sixth day of the bright fortnight called ‘Skandaṣaṣṭhī’ is an important festival observed especially in South India.

asamprajñāta
(‘ultra-cognitive absorption’)
------------------------------------------
Out of the षड्-दर्शनस् or six systems of इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य्, that of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) known as the Yoga-sūtras, is very popular since it gives highly practical methods of controlling the मिन्द्.
When a systematic attempt is made to control and eliminate the vṛttis or modifications of the मिन्द् through the practice of the various steps of योग such as यम and नियम, it will result in ‘samādhi,’ total absorption in the object of contemplation.
This समाधि is of two types: sam-prajñāta (cognitive) and असम्प्रज्ञात (ultra-cognitive). In the former, the object of contemplation will be vividly revealed. In this state, though all other mental modifications are eliminated, that of the object of contemplation continues to remain active. Hence in the strictest sense of the definition of ‘yoga’ as ‘cittavṛtti-nirodha’ (Yogasūtras 1.2) (‘suppression of modifications of मिन्द्’) this समाधि indicates a lower state of योग. As opposed to this, in the higher समाधि called असम्प्रज्ञात, all modifications of मिन्द् are eliminated, leaving only the सṁस्कारस् (latent tendencies) behind. (vide योग-sūtras 1.18). In this state, it looks as though even the मिन्द् does not exist, since there are no mental modifications to reveal its presence.
This समाधि is sometimes called ‘nirbīja-समाधि’ (seedless समाधि) since the seeds of rebirth are eliminated as a result of this experience.
Intense वैराग्य (‘paravairāgya’) or detachment is said to be the means of achieving this समाधि.
See also YOGADARŚANA.

āsana
(‘posture’, ‘seat’)
------------------------------------------
Though āsanas are a very popular mode of exercise, the word ‘āsana’ has a much wider connotation and deeper signi-ficance. पतञ्जलि, the great master of योग, has listed आसन as the third of the eight steps of योग. According to him, any posture in which the योगि can sit steadily and comfortably, is ‘āsana.’ This आसन can be mastered through meditation on the infinite and by a relaxation of the body and मिन्द्. When this technique of आसन is perfected, the योगि acquires immunity from the effects of pairs of opposites like heat and cold, hunger and thirst, happiness and misery (vide योग-sūtras 2.46, 47 and 48). Out of the six āsanas that are recommended as suitable for meditation, पद्मासन and svasti-kāsana are supposed to be the best.
Āsanas as physical postures come under the purview of another branch of योग, known as ‘Haṭhyoga.’ These āsanas, it is claimed, can cure diseases, improve health and help in meditation. Though the typical posture of every living being can serve as a model for an आसन, only 84 āsanas are handed down in tradition as especially suitable for human beings. Out of these again, only 32 are more in vogue.
Āsana can also mean a seat. Various kinds of seats have been recommended as suitable for meditation. Seats made of कुश grass, deer-skin, tiger-skin, woollen rug or silk cloth have been mentioned in the works on योग, along with the fruits one will get by using them.
See also YOGADARŚANA and YOGĀSANAS.

āśaya
(‘that which rests [in the मिन्द्]’)
------------------------------------------
Hinduism believes in rebirth. The सोउल् of any being, though immortal, continues to be born again and again due to its कर्म or the subtle unseen deserts. This goes on until it gets मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् from this cycle of births and deaths.
It is this ‘karma’ that has been called ‘āśaya’ or ‘karmāśaya’ by some scriptures like the Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (1.24; 2.12). It has been called ‘āśaya’ since it ‘rests in the मिन्द्’ (śaya = resting) ‘until’ (ā = until) it fructifies. It is of the form of पुण्य (merit) and पाप (de-merit) and is generated by काम (desire), लोभ (greed), मोह (delusion) and krodha (anger). Its results may be experienced either in this life itself or in future births.

asamavāyi-kāraṇa
(‘non-inherent cause’)
------------------------------------------
The वैशेषिक दर्शन (a logical system of इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य् attributed to the sage कणाद) recognizes seven padārthas or categories of reality, out of which समवाय or the relation of inhe-rence forms the sixth. It is the eternal relationship that subsists between the whole and the parts, the quality or an action and the substance possessing or doing it and so on.
Clay is the material cause for the jug. The two are inseparable. Hence, clay is called the samavāyi-कारण, an inherent cause, of the jug. However, the colour of the jug is not caused by the clay, but by the colour of the clay which again exists in clay by समवाय. Hence, the colour of the clay is said to be the असमवायि-कारण, a non-inherent cause, of the colour of the jug.

asatkāryavāda
(‘the theory of non-existent effect’)
------------------------------------------
The relationship between a cause (like clay) and its effect (like the pot) has provided enough material for discussion in इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य्. Several theories have been advocated in which this relationship has been sought to be explained. ‘Asat-कार्य-वाद’ is the theory that has been put forward by the schools of बुद्धिस्म् and of न्याय-Vaiśeṣikas.
When the pot, the effect, is produced from clay, its cause, two explanations are possible. The effect, which already existed in its cause in a subtle form, was mani-fested when favourable circumstances were created; because a real effect cannot be produced from an unreal or non-existing cause. This theory is called ‘satkāryavāda’ and is advocated generally by the Sāṅkhya system. The other explanation is that the effect, which is something new, is produced as a result of the efforts of the potter and his implements, even though it did not exist earlier. If the clay and the pot were not different from each other, we should have used the same name for both and they should have served the same purpose. But this is not so. Hence according to this view, a real effect (‘kārya’) is produced from the cause though it did not exist earlier (hence unreal or ‘asat’) in that cause. Therefore the name ‘asatkārya-वाद.’
